#178503. Motorcycles are notoriously dangerous. Could electric motorcycles actually change that?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1736 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Motorcycles are notoriously dangerous. Could electric motorcycles actually change that?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1736 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, there’s no particularly comfortable way to talk about motorcycle safety.
  • In a recent development, but that simple statement also hides something key.
  • Not because electricity is somehow safer than gasoline.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, there’s no particularly comfortable way to talk about motorcycle safety. Motorcycles are dangerous. All the statistics point to the fact that per mile, motorcycles are significantly more dangerous. And as someone who promotes them as a better alternative to large cars and trucks for many trips, it’s an uncomfortable reality that must be grappled with.

In a recent development, but that simple statement also hides something key. Not all motorcycles, riders, or riding behaviors carry the same risk. And as a fresh generation of smaller electric motorcycles begins to emerge, I think there’s an interesting question worth asking: Could electric motorcycles inadvertently make motorcycling safer?

Not because electricity is somehow safer than gasoline. It isn’t. Rather, because electrification may fundamentally change the type of motorcycle that hits the road.

In 2024, 6,228 motorcyclists were killed in the US, accounting for 16% of all traffic fatalities, according to the NHTSA.

Obviously, motorcycles have a fundamental disadvantage here. You don’t have a steel cage around you. There aren’t crumple zones separating your body from an oncoming SUV. There’s no seatbelt holding you in place or curtain airbag waiting to catch your head.

But there’s another component to motorcycle fatalities that is harder to ignore: rider behavior.

Recent findings suggest that around 35% of motorcyclist deaths in 2024 occurred in single-vehicle crashes, according to the IIHS. In other words, more than one-third of those deaths didn’t involve a rider being hit by another vehicle. At that point, whether or not a crash occurred was essentially in the hands of the rider.

Alcohol is another major factor. Among riders killed in single-vehicle crashes, the NHTSA reports that 40% were alcohol-impaired.

Then there are the bikes themselves.

Supersport motorcycles stand out for all the wrong reasons. Of the riders killed on supersports in 2024, 59% were under 30. Compare that to cruiser and standard motorcycles, where just 19% of killed riders were under 30, or touring motorcycles at only 7%.

According to recent reports, that’s not proof that powerful motorcycles are causing those deaths, of course. There are all sorts of confounding factors, including the type of person attracted to different motorcycles and how those motorcycles tend to be ridden.

But it’s hard to ignore the broader picture.

Sources indicate that to put it more plainly, a huge portion of motorcycle deaths are caused by riders simply going too fast, doing something wrong (like drinking or taking turns too aggressively), or because they couldn’t handle the power of an insanely high-performance crotch rocket. So while figures such as “motorcycles are 27x more deadly than cars” might be true in a broad sense, that doesn’t mean you have a 27x higher chance of death – especially not if you aren’t a 25-year-old hooligan on a second-hand liter bike.

One of the strange things about motorcycling is just how cheaply you can buy extraordinary performance.

Sources indicate that someone with relatively little riding experience can buy a used supersport capable of acceleration that would have required an exotic supercar not long ago. The motorcycle may weigh around 400 lb, produce well over 100 horsepower, and be capable of speeds approaching three times a typical US highway speed limit.

And unlike cars, there isn’t much protecting you when that performance gets away from you.

That’s why I find the current evolution of electric motorcycles so interesting.

For years, electric motorcycle companies largely chased gasoline motorcycles up the performance ladder. We got incredibly fast and powerful machines from companies like Energica and LiveWire.

Those bikes proved electric motorcycles could be fast.

But I’m increasingly interested in the opposite end of the spectrum.

Look at motorcycles such as LiveWire’s upcoming S4 Honcho.

This isn’t an electric superbike designed around insane acceleration or a 150 mph (240 km/h) top speed. It’s a smaller motorcycle intended to offer approachable performance at a more accessible price.

It adds to a growing market already populated by highly acclaimed modest-sized electric motorcycles like those from Ryvid, Land, and Maeving.

And we’re seeing more machines begin to occupy this previously neglected territory between an e-bike and a full-size motorcycle.

That could make a huge difference when it comes to overall safety, as crotch rockets get replaced by sensible electric motorbikes.

In a recent development, battery technology actually creates an interesting incentive here. Making an electric motorcycle ridiculously powerful is easy. Giving it enough battery to sustain high speeds for long distances without becoming extremely heavy and expensive is much, much harder.

So the economics and physics of batteries naturally make smaller urban and suburban motorcycles fairly compelling right now.

Instead of asking how to build another 150 mph (240 km/h) electric motorcycle, manufacturers can build a lighter machine that goes 60 or 70 mph (95-120 km/h), has enough range for everyday riding, and costs considerably less.

Ironically, one of the limitations most commonly leveled against electric motorcycles could turn out to have a safety upside.

This is where I think things get even more interesting.

Sources indicate that for decades, the stereotypical progression into motorcycling might have involved learning on a dirt bike or small displacement motorcycle, then moving fairly swiftly into larger machines. Often though, upcoming riders simply took a licensing course and then bought their first 600cc sport bike to learn to ride.

But now we’re raising an entirely upcoming generation on electric two-wheelers.

Kids and teenagers are increasingly growing up riding e-bikes and small electric motos. Eventually, many of them are going to want something faster than a 20 or 28 mph e-bike.

Industry observers note that A 50 mph (80 km/h) electric motorcycle is a pretty logical next step for the e-moto kids of today. Eventually, perhaps that rider graduates to something capable of 70 or 80 mph (120-130 km/h) and comfortable highway travel.

That’s a much more gradual performance curve than jumping from essentially no powered two-wheeler experience to a screaming 600cc supersport.

Recent findings suggest that there’s another advantage too: electric motorcycles are mechanically easier to operate. There’s generally no clutch, no gearbox, and no concern about stalling. Twist the throttle and go.

That doesn’t necessarily make them safer – instant electric torque can certainly get an inexperienced rider into trouble – but it does remove several tasks from the mental workload of learning to ride.

It has been revealed that the rider can spend more attention on braking, cornering, traffic, positioning, and the thousand other things that actually keep you alive on a motorcycle. The reduction in cognitive load can mean more focus on control, if it’s used that way.

To be clear, I’m not arguing that electric motorcycles are inherently safe.

Industry observers note that they’re still motorcycles and they still lack cages. Well, most of them.

If an inattentive driver turns left in front of you, the chemistry powering your rear wheel isn’t going to make much difference.

And electric motorcycles can be outrageously powerful. In fact, the instantaneous torque of an electric motor can make poor throttle calibration especially unforgiving for inexperienced riders.

There also simply isn’t enough data yet to demonstrate that electric motorcycles have meaningfully lower fatality rates than comparable gasoline motorcycles.

But that’s not really my argument.

My argument is that electrification may change what we consider a normal beginner motorcycle. And that could be much more vital, helping to significantly reduce accidents and deaths.

Industry observers note that I’m never going to pretend motorcycles can become as safe as cars. The physics simply don’t work that way.

But the broad statistic of “motorcycles are dangerous” encompasses an enormous spectrum of machines and riders.

A sober, trained commuter wearing proper protective gear and riding a modestly powered motorcycle to work is doing something fundamentally different from an inexperienced 21-year-old seeing how fast his supersport can take an empty freeway ramp at 2 a.m.

Yet both contribute to the same broad motorcycle fatality statistics.

What excites me about this emerging generation of electric motorcycles isn’t that swapping gasoline for batteries magically fixes motorcycle safety. It obviously doesn’t.

I bought a motorcycle around age 60 after considering the risk factors I could control:.

Industry observers note that I took a MSF basic riding course before buying the motorcycle. Best investment in the whole saga.

Industry observers note that I never rode impaired. That was easy.

I always rode with full protection. That was doable but inconvenient and seriously uncomfortable in hot weather.

In a recent development, I never rode in rainy weather or at night. Again possible but limited my use of the motorcycle for commuting. Eventually my schedule changed to evening and stopped my motorcycle commuting altogether.

After a few close calls I started avoiding roads with more than one lane in each direction. That added quite a bit to my commute time.

I never rode when I was in a hurry. That meant more days I didn't use the motorcycle for commuting.

Sources indicate that none of these precautions have anything to do with electric drive. After I sold my gas motorcycle I test rode an electric motorcycle and loved it. However I didn't buy it because it didn't reduce any of the risks and I wouldn't ride it more than the gas bike.

It’s that electrification could help create a new category of desirable, affordable motorcycles that don’t need 120 horsepower and a 160 mph top speed to be cool.

If younger riders grow up progressing from e-bikes to small e-motos and then to highway-capable electric motorcycles, perhaps we’ll wind up with a generation that sees a lightweight 60 or 70 mph motorcycle as a perfectly legitimate machine rather than merely a stepping stone to something ridiculously powerful.

Maybe electrification’s biggest contribution to motorcycle safety won’t be traction control, ABS, or sophisticated electronics.

Maybe it’ll simply make sensible motorcycles fun and cool again.

#178502. Tech Report: Why Sleep Consistency May Be the Missing Piece When It Comes to Heart Health

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1749 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Womenshealthmag ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Why Sleep Consistency May Be the Missing Piece When It Comes to Heart Health

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1749 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that you probably already know that getting seven to nine hours of sleep each night is one of the best things you can do for your health and wellbeing.
  • In a recent development, as it turns out, your heart might not be too happy about that.
  • Before you start stressing over every late night or weekend sleep-in, though, there's some important context to understand.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that you probably already know that getting seven to nine hours of sleep each night is one of the best things you can do for your health and wellbeing. But what happens if you’re consistently hitting that goal while going to bed at different times? Think 10 p.m. on Monday, midnight on Wednesday, and well past 1 a.m. on Saturday because it’s the weekend, after all.

In a recent development, as it turns out, your heart might not be too happy about that. New research suggests that sleep consistency—which includes both when you go to bed and wake up, and how much sleep you get from night to night—could play an important role in cardiovascular health. And, while getting the recommended amount of shut-eye still matters, researchers are finding that how much your sleep fluctuates may deserve some attention, too.

Before you start stressing over every late night or weekend sleep-in, though, there's some important context to understand. Here's what the research actually found, why your body seems to care so much about routine, and how consistent your sleep schedule really needs to be.

In a recent development, meet the experts: Nguyen Minh Tuan Viet, MD, PhD, is a neuroscientist and postdoctoral research fellow at Boston Children's Hospital and Harvard Medical School and lead researcher of the newly introduced study. Nour Makarem, PhD, is a cardiovascular epidemiologist in the department of epidemiology at Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health. Marie-Pierre St-Onge, PhD, is a professor of nutritional medicine and director of the Center of Excellence for Sleep & Circadian Research at Columbia University Irving Medical Center.

For the latest study published in Circulation: Cardiovascular Quality and Outcomes, researchers analyzed more than one million nights of sleep data from 10,362 adults participating in the National Institutes of Health's All of Us Research Program, an initiative that aims to collect data from over one million Americans and create the country’s largest biomedical database.

Unlike previous studies that only looked at people's sleep habits for about a week, this one used about six months of Fitbit data to see how participants' bedtimes, wake-up times, and total sleep duration changed from night to night. They then compared those patterns with participants’ medical records and tracked their health for nearly four years.

The findings were pretty eye-opening: For every additional 29 minutes of variation in how long someone slept from night to night, their relative risk of serious heart problems, including heart attacks, heart failure, heart muscle disease, and certain strokes, was 24 percent higher. To be clear, that doesn't mean going to bed 29 minutes later than usual on a given night increases your heart disease risk by 24 percent. The researchers were looking at a statistical measure of how much someone's total sleep duration varied over time, rather than the consequences of one late bedtime. As of now, all this information does it point to a potential link between sleep schedule variation and heart disease.

Researchers also found that greater night-to-night fluctuations in bedtime and wake-up times were associated with a 23 percent and 20 percent higher relative risk of cardiovascular problems, respectively. This means that both the consistency of your sleep schedule and the consistency of the duration of that sleep may play a role in heart health.

Sources indicate that there are a few things worth keeping in mind, though. For starters, this study found a connection between inconsistent sleep and heart problems, but it couldn't prove that irregular sleep is what causes those problems. In fact, Viet points out that the relationship could work in the opposite direction too (i.e. early illness might actually make someone’s sleep more irregular). Plus, most participants were women and white, so we can't necessarily assume the findings apply to everyone. Still, the results add to growing evidence that sleep consistency deserves a place in the heart-health conversation.

According to recent reports, your body has its own internal clock, known as your circadian rhythm, which determines when you're tired, when you're wide awake, and even how bodily functions like blood pressure and heart rate change throughout the day. And, it works at its best when it has a reasonably predictable schedule to follow. When you're constantly changing when you sleep and wake, you may disrupt that rhythm, a phenomenon known as circadian misalignment, explains Nour Makarem, PhD, a cardiovascular epidemiologist in the department of epidemiology at Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health.

That disruption can impact some pretty notable cardiovascular processes, like how your body regulates blood pressure. Under normal circumstances, blood pressure usually drops by about 10 to 20 percent while you're sleeping to give your cardiovascular system a period of rest, but research by Makarem suggests that irregular sleep patterns may be associated with higher blood pressure and an increased risk of hypertension. “This is problematic because higher nocturnal blood pressure and having a non-dipping profile (blood pressure that does not dip or dip enough during sleep) are associated with higher risk for heart disease and stroke, the leading causes of death in women,” she indicates.

It has been revealed that your sleep schedule may also interact with other daily rhythms, including when you eat and exercise. These behaviors help regulate biological clocks throughout your body, including those involved in metabolism, Makarem says. When those clocks fall out of sync, processes like blood sugar regulation may be affected, too. In fact, research has linked irregular sleep patterns with poorer glucose regulation and a higher risk of metabolic concerns.

It has been revealed that research is still emerging, but scientists are noticing some important links between sleep consistency and heart health. A 2025 study published in the Journal of Epidemiology & Community Health followed more than 72,000 adults and found that people with irregular sleep patterns had a higher risk of major cardiovascular events, including heart attacks and strokes. Another study published in Sleep in 2024 analyzed sleep patterns in more than 60,000 adults and found that sleep regularity was a stronger predictor of mortality risk than sleep duration in that population.

In a recent development, so, does this mean having a consistent bed and rising time matters more than getting eight hours? Not necessarily. "The evidence for sleep regularity is rather nascent relative to that for sleep duration," says Marie-Pierre St-Onge, PhD, a professor of nutritional medicine and director of the Center of Excellence for Sleep & Circadian Research at Columbia University Irving Medical Center. She explains that while several studies have made the connection between irregular sleep and poorer health outcomes, more research needs to be done to determine whether making someone's sleep schedule more consistent can actually lower their cardiovascular risk. And, we do have plenty of evidence that getting enough sleep has positive affects on just about every system in the body, from brain function to muscle recovery.

Overall, there are still things researchers are learning about sleep consistency and heart health, but it’s safe to start thinking of it as another piece of the puzzle, alongside getting enough hours and making sure those hours are restorative.

Sources indicate that here's the million-dollar question: Does protecting your heart mean going to bed at exactly 10:30 p.m. every single night, no exceptions? Thankfully, no.

Recent findings suggest that ultimately, you’ve got some wiggle room. "In general, we would recommend that individuals try not to deviate by 60 min up or down from their average bedtime or sleep duration," claims St-Onge, but the smaller the gap, the better.

It has been revealed that think of that as a target, not a hard-and-fast rule. An occasional late night or weekend sleep-in isn’t a reason to panic. What matters more is establishing a reasonably consistent pattern over a period of time rather than expecting yourself to follow a perfect schedule every single night.

Industry observers note that if you've had a particularly short night, St-Onge recommends trying to go to bed a little earlier and waking up a little later when your schedule allows, rather than trying to make up for all that lost sleep by sleeping in for hours. Most importantly, don't sweat it. "If one night is off, it's not all doom and gloom; you get right back on schedule the following night," notes St-Onge.

Here are a few small changes experts recommend to improve your sleep routine without completely overhauling your lifestyle.

Recent findings suggest that before committing to being in bed every night by 9 p.m., consider what will actually make sense for your schedule. Earlier isn't automatically better. What's important is getting adequate sleep on a schedule that works with your body's natural rhythm and everyday responsibilities, explains St-Onge.

In a recent development, if your current bedtime is midnight but you'd ideally like to be asleep by 11, there's no need to make that change all at once. Makarem recommends gradually shifting your bedtime earlier by about 10 minutes each day until you reach your target. The idea is to give your body time to adjust rather than suddenly expecting yourself to fall asleep an hour earlier than usual.

It's tempting to stay up late on Friday and Saturday nights and make up for it by sleeping well into the morning, but even those brief changes can leave you feeling out of sync by the time Monday rolls around. If possible, St-Onge recommends keeping your weekend bedtimes within about an hour of your usual routine.

If you wear an Apple Watch or Fitbit to bed, you know how easy it is to get caught up in the numbers. One morning you're celebrating a great sleep score, and the next you're wondering what went wrong because your tracker says you barely got any deep sleep.

While these devices can be helpful for spotting patterns, the last thing you want is to start losing sleep over your sleep. Makarem recommends using trackers to keep tabs on your habits or remind you when it's time for bed, but only if they're actually helping. If checking your sleep stats is making you anxious, it's fine to ditch the data and simply pay attention to when you're going to bed and waking up.

Sources indicate that and remember, you don't have to get your sleep schedule exactly right every single night to do something good for your heart. Small changes that you can actually stick with are worth more than chasing a perfect score. As Makarem puts it, "Progress is better than perfect.".

9 rescued orangutans returned to the wild in Indonesia

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the Indonesian province of West Kalimantan, on the island of Borneo, is no stranger to wildfires.
  • In a recent development, earlier this year, four mother-baby orangutan pairs and one adult female orangutan (genus Pongo) were rescued from areas in Ketapang (a regency in the West Kalimantan province) impacted by the fires.
  • In a recent development, they were taken to an orangutan rescue and rehabilitation centre in Ketapang, West Kalimantan.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the Indonesian province of West Kalimantan, on the island of Borneo, is no stranger to wildfires. Horrific wildfires burned in 2015 and 2019, the latter of which set ablaze around 1.6 million hectares of Indonesian forest and land. However, the scale of destruction from this year’s El Niño-intensified fires throughout the island is unprecedented, according to the nonprofit International Animal Rescue.

In a recent development, earlier this year, four mother-baby orangutan pairs and one adult female orangutan (genus Pongo) were rescued from areas in Ketapang (a regency in the West Kalimantan province) impacted by the fires. They were dehydrated and malnourished, and some had burned their feet, likely because they stepped on embers as they crossed burning peatland.

In a recent development, they were taken to an orangutan rescue and rehabilitation centre in Ketapang, West Kalimantan. The center is run by Yayasan Inisiasi Alam Rehabilitasi Indonesia (YIARI), a nonprofit dedicated to primate and habitat conservation in Indonesia. YIARI’s medical team kept an eye on their recovery, and then conducted health examinations to make sure they were all ready for release. The last of these examinations revealed that three of the females were pregnant.

“Their return to the wild is therefore especially crucial, giving these mothers the opportunity to raise their future young in a safer forest habitat,” International Animal Rescue, YIARI’s founding partner, wrote in a statement.

It has been revealed that experts ultimately chose to release them at Batu Nyambu Protected Forest. While also in West Kalimantan, its roughly 23,000 hectares of land and nearby forests haven’t been affected by the recent fires. Batu Nyambu has plenty of natural food, fresh water, nesting trees, and space. But getting the females and their babies there wasn’t simple—they had to travel by road, boat, and on foot for a total of 12 hours. Luckily, they had support from local communities and traditional leaders.

Sources indicate that “We are grateful for the support of the community, village governments and traditional leaders,” said Argitoe Ranting, YIARI’s Director of Operations. “The long-term success of conservation efforts depends not only on protecting the area, but also on the role of the people living around the forest in safeguarding habitat and preventing various threats to wildlife.”.

Most fires in Indonesia are associated with human activity such as using fire to clear land for plantations and agriculture.

When you're short on space (or even if you're not), having an extra set of drawers on hand is a huge boon for small bedrooms. That's where the best storage beds come in. I'm all about bedroom furniture that does more for your sleep setup, so I gathered up a few favorites from the AD staff. These storage bed picks include sleek, streamlined designs with completely concealed side storage, queen- and king-size beds with pullouts at the footboard, and more. Each one stows generously while you sleep.

It has been revealed that A storage bed frame need not be ugly, even if function is the whole point of buying one. In fact, I tapped other editors and we found impressive wooden beds from Thuma and West Elm, the upholstered storage beds of our minimalist dreams from Saatva, Article, and Sundays, and a lilac velvet showpiece from CB2 for anyone who wants their storage bed to be the loudest thing in the room. Sources indicate that to truly give these recommendations on the best storage beds, I featured options that include a variety of price points, storage features, designs, and more to guide you on your own shopping journey. Read more on the key factors other writers and I kept in mind below:.

Delivery and Assembly: The last thing you want is to wait months for your bed frame to help you organize (and elevate) your space. We selected options that offer reasonable shipping windows (usually within one month from placing your order to its arrival at your home) as well as white glove delivery to help set up the storage bed in your desired room, or a frame simple enough to assemble yourself.

Design: A substantial passion of ours at AD is finding furniture that is not only functional but is also not an eyesore. We skipped clunky bed frames and included pieces that can sit comfortably anywhere in modern and minimalist bedrooms and beyond.

Size: Our editors tested a mix of queen and king sizes, and prices in this story reflect queens. We looked for picks that come in a range of sizes to accommodate any space. Keep in mind that storage beds often have features like pull-out drawers and lift-up bases, so be sure to measure your space and compare it to your desired storage bed's dimensions to ensure the bed can open properly in your bedroom.

Storage Features: The storage bed you select should align with your space. If you're tight on floor space, consider a storage bed that lifts up. If you have low ceilings, consider a storage bed that has drawers underneath.

Durability: We tested storage beds by sleeping on them night after night, taking notice of any factors like creakiness or wobbliness. We also looked for options with high-quality materials like fine upholstery and solid wood that are designed to last.

Industry observers note that price: Storage beds run from a few hundred dollars to well over $2,000, and our picks span that whole range. While the price isn't always the biggest indicator of quality, materials like bouclé and solid wood are usually found in more high-end storage beds.

What Are the Different Types of Storage Beds?

Lift-up beds: Also called an "ottoman bed," this is a model where the mattress base lifts up with the aid of gas struts (pressurized cylinders that do most of the lifting for you), which retailers often call hydraulic lifts. This typically offers the most room out of the storage bed options.

Drawer beds: Fairly self-explanatory: drawers (either under, alongside, or at the foot of the bed) are this frame’s storage approach.

Sources indicate that headboard storage beds: A headboard storage bed draws from mid-century styles, where built-in shelves or nightstands create storage opportunities. This is a good option if what you need to store is also aesthetically pleasing.

Cubby beds: Instead of drawers, these cubbies are open shelving solutions underneath the bed frame, particularly suitable for holding books if you’re looking for a stylish way to create a bedroom library.

What’s a “Hydraulic Lift” in a Storage Bed?

When your storage bed has interior storage (in other words, when you lift the mattress base upward to access its storage), it needs a lift mechanism to make it possible for you to lift the bed without breaking your back, and to keep the slatted frame upright while you lift your items in and out. Most use gas struts, though you'll often see them sold as hydraulic. If your storage bed has interior storage and no lift, you will collapse yourself and ultimately be pancaked by your own sleep-and-store investment.

What Features Should I Look for in the Best Storage Beds?

Recent findings suggest that A good storage bed, in our opinion, doesn't look like a storage bed. It looks like a regular bed. It's crafted from, ideally, kiln-dried hardwood, it has a slatted base so you don't need to bother with a box spring, and it has non-sticky drawers (thank you, Thuma) or a lift mechanism to help with the lifting of interior storage (thank you, Saatva). Look for a solid wood base, linen upholstery, and invest in some vacuum-sealed bags. I live by these.

What Materials Make a Good Storage Bed?

It has been revealed that you're primarily searching for durability and space in storage bed models. Look for frames made from solid wood since this type of material is typically sturdy and long-lasting. A lift mechanism makes storage more accessible without back-breaking exercises. While upholstered beds are a popular favorite, make sure what lies beneath the textile is also going to stand the test of time.

Is Cheating in Marriage Ever Justified?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (798 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.
  • “Yes, cheating can damage a marriage,” a couples therapist I interviewed a few years ago told me, “yet it can also make the marriage stronger.”.
  • Most of us generally would not recommend such an activity, as we know that while fire can warm your home, it can also burn your house down.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.

“Yes, cheating can damage a marriage,” a couples therapist I interviewed a few years ago told me, “yet it can also make the marriage stronger.”.

This approach is playing with fire. Most of us generally would not recommend such an activity, as we know that while fire can warm your home, it can also burn your house down. Instead, we would more likely suggest learning how to use fire responsibly—for the warming and cooking, not the burning.

Sources indicate that we could also compare cheating on your spouse with taking care of your health. Living through cancer can become the catalyst for making better decisions about how to live your life. Yet I wouldn't recommend smoking two packs a day to attempt to induce this appreciation—as it can also lead to another outcome.

In a recent development, it’s the same with relationships. Betrayal can become the catalyst for candid discussions about what hasn’t been working, open conversations about intimacy, and a renewed appreciation of what you have. Alternatively, it can lead to the loss of the relationship—the scorched-house equivalent of playing with fire.

Industry observers note that after infidelity, both people become aware that the other person was willing to take this risk. All the post-cheating epiphanies do not erase this awareness, and it feels extremely painful and difficult to assimilate for the person who was betrayed.

Why is this? Cheating is the ultimate form of narcissistic validation. It’s a trade: your short-term validation for your partner’s long-term suffering.

And suffer they will. “I will regret it for the rest of my life,” shares one woman in a recent survey. “My marriage was already falling apart, but I will never forget the look of hurt on my now ex-husband's face when he found out. He forgave me many years ago, but I still struggle to forgive myself some twenty-plus years later.”.

To understand the problem with betraying your intimate partner, consider the words of Afghan-American novelist Khaled Hosseini. “There is only one sin, only one, and that is theft. Every other sin is a variation of theft,” shares Hosseini in The Kite Runner. “When you kill a man, you steal a life. You steal his wife’s right of a husband, you rob his children of a father. When you lie you steal someone’s right to truth. When you cheat, you steal the right to fairness.”.

To make matters worse, when you betray another human being, it’s not just the right to fairness you are taking from them. You also take their right to believe in love, in acceptance, in belonging.

Recent findings suggest that in other words, you take everything that most matters to them. “There is no more wretched act than stealing,” Hosseini concludes.

Industry observers note that “At the end of the day, it wasn’t the cheating that hurt the most,” confides another woman, “it was the betrayal. Someone I trusted so much didn't trust me enough to simply say, ‘Hey, I'm unhappy, and I want out.’”.

Despite the harm we do to others, in our fragile, volatile search for validation, many of us are capable of seeing past how infidelity will affect the other person. We often don’t see the forest when standing right in front of a tree. We don’t think about the trust that will be eroded, and almost always never fully recaptured, if we cheat.

It has been revealed that why? Trust in a relationship is like air. You don’t think about air unless you don’t have it. Then it becomes the only thing you think about.

When you convince another human being to build their life around you and then take that safety and security from them through betrayal, you dispel the closest approximation to sacredness you will ever experience in your life.

It is at this point that you learn that when you destroy what is sacred, you destroy the sacred within you.

In a recent development, cheating, then, is not only an ethically flawed form of validation; it also injures ourselves. We need to find better ways to express our relationship dissatisfaction.

If your partner is unable to listen to you or adapt with you for a protracted period, separation may be a recourse. It’s very simple: If you can’t continue your commitment, tell them rather than going down the road of pretend. They deserve as much from you.

Once you’ve come clean, you can move in another direction in your intimate life—and seek the Holy Grail of external validation you’ve been craving—knowing you were honest and did what you could to preserve the sacred within your relationship.

Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: The Good and the Hard of Life on GLP-1s

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that “Years of diets that worked for a couple of months, then gave all the weight back and more.
  • In June, our brilliant News team published a piece about actor Mayim Bialik and her challenging experience with GLP-1 side effects.
  • Jump forward nearly 4 months; our equally brilliant social media team posts the piece on Facebook, leading with one of Bialik’s quotes from the article: “GLP-1s have helped people in serious need.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that “Years of diets that worked for a couple of months, then gave all the weight back and more. Now the food noise has gone quiet,” a GLP-1 user shared.

In June, our brilliant News team published a piece about actor Mayim Bialik and her challenging experience with GLP-1 side effects. It did well, like many of the celebrity + health condition + human-interest angle features we create tend to do with our audience (that’s you all reading this!). Not a massive viral hit by any measure, but a strong performer on the traffic front.

Life in a busy newsroom went on.

Jump forward nearly 4 months; our equally brilliant social media team posts the piece on Facebook, leading with one of Bialik’s quotes from the article: “GLP-1s have helped people in serious need. Of that I am certain. But nobody talks much about what happens when it goes wrong.”.

It has been revealed that the fuse was lit. Nearly 12k likes, 1k reposts, and 3.5k comments later, the team had their most engaged post of the year by some margin. The irony is not lost on me that Bialik’s quote, about how rarely people talk about side effects, sparked such a deep conversation about that very thing.

It has been revealed that GLP-1s are a massive topic for Healthline. They drive traffic, they drive revenue, and they offer a rich seam of human-centric storytelling for our teams. Even so, no one predicted the post would catch fire the way it did. Our social team’s read is that a few things stacked up: Mayim Bialik is a name our Facebook audience knows, the topic is one where nearly everyone has a stake, and a busy thread tends to get shown to more people, who then add more comments. That’s the hypothesis. What we’ve consistently seen is that posts that lead with a quote get more people talking than those that lead with a headline. You may have noticed this article takes the same approach.

We also know that the comment sections on social media aren’t always the most hospitable of environments, particularly in the health space. What stood out about the lion’s share of the comments we read was how constructive the discourse was. People were leading with deeply personal and often moving perspectives about the life changing impact (for good and bad) of GLP-1s. In turn, they were met with equally balanced and thoughtful responses.

Sources indicate that many of the comments expanded on Bialik’s experience, detailing long and difficult battles with a range of side effects. But plenty told the other side of the story: years of failed diets and struggles with chronic conditions leading to despondency, side effects that went on to ease with time, and life changing results that were ultimately worth the cost.

The line that opened this piece could have come from any of those commenters. It didn’t. It came from Kitty Hough, who is 75 and lives in London. Eagle-eyed readers will have spotted that she has the same surname as me – that’s because she’s my mom. She’s one of two people closer to the Healthline home who spoke to me for this piece and whose stories echo the Facebook post thread, with the good and the hard bits side by side.

In a recent development, kitty was a hockey player and distance runner as a girl, the kind who could eat what she liked without it showing. Then came children, and a weight that crept up year after year, with decades of diets that “worked for a couple of months only to be back to my former weight and then some.” In late 2024, after a lot of research, she decided to try tirzepatide.

Since then, Kitty has lost 56 pounds. She claims her joints hurt less, which she puts down to reduced inflammation. She is more mobile. The constant chatter about food has faded. She thinks harder before she eats now.

“I am a strong believer that obesity is a disease and in my case certainly not the result of overindulgence or laziness,” she says. “GLP-1s have greatly improved my health and self-esteem. After years of struggling with my weight, I have finally found a way to solve the problem.”.

In a recent development, kitty will also tell you what it cost. Nausea. Constipation. Sulfur-tasting burps and rough nights of indigestion. Initial hair loss that has since grown back, and loose skin. Muscle loss. And she misses some of the true joy of cooking and eating food.

But despite bumps in her journey, Kitty remains convinced that the benefits of GLP-1s for her life and health outweigh any drawbacks she’s experienced. “I am conscious that I will probably be on this drug for a long time if not for life. It is truly a miracle drug.”.

I also spoke to Ann Marie Maguire, AGNP-C, RN, TCTCN, a nurse practitioner specializing in transplantation and cellular therapy, the sister of Healthline’s Chief Business Officer Christine Macguire, and someone who has lost over 50lbs since starting GLP-1s in 2022.

“I struggled with my weight since my teens and always believed I should be able to manage it on my own. But in my 30s, my knees were hurting just getting out of bed or walking to dinner. I realized how much my weight was affecting my quality of life. Starting a GLP-1 in 2022, alongside healthier eating and exercise, made a tremendous difference. My only regret is not starting sooner,” stated Ann Marie.

As a healthcare professional, Ann Marie also identified cost as a major factor that can’t be ignored regarding GLP-1s and their impact.

Recent findings suggest that “There’s understandable debate about the long-term use and cost of these medications,” she says. “But we also need to consider the health and financial burden of obesity, including cardiovascular complications, hospitalizations, surgeries and ongoing medications. The cost conversation should account for the potential benefits of preventing or reducing those complications.”.

Ann Marie points to a frustration many patients will recognize: reaching a healthier weight can become the reason coverage gets cut off. “We don’t automatically stop blood pressure medication because a patient’s readings improve,” she claims. The treatment may be what’s keeping the condition controlled. Obesity, she argues, deserves the same approach. “Reaching a goal weight can mean treatment is working, and decisions about continuing it should reflect the patient’s ongoing needs, benefits and side effects.”.

It’s vital to note that this article looks at the experiences of only a handful of people out of the millions who now take GLP-1s. Like all drugs, these medications are not right for everyone. Side effects are common; some of them can be serious, and both the long-term impact and what happens when people stop are still being worked out. Ultimately, your care team, with knowledge of your medical history, is a far better guide than a comment thread.

Yet the evidence now reaches well beyond the scales: large trials have linked semaglutide to fewer heart attacks and strokes in people with heart disease and slower kidney decline in people with diabetes and kidney disease, and tirzepatide became the first FDA-approved drug for moderate to severe sleep apnea in adults with obesity.

Stories like Kitty’s, Ann Marie’s, Mayim Bialik’s, and those of the 3.5k commenters on the Facebook post aren’t proof of what will happen to you one way or another. But for a lot of people, my mom included, these drugs have changed what an ordinary day looks like, and in many cases changed what their future can look like.

One of the most significant drug developments of the century so far? Hard to argue with.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Wednesday in our Healthline Wellness Wire newsletter.

Industry observers note that the VW ID. Polo Trend with the 37 kWh battery went on sale in Europe in July, starting at just 24,995 euros, or about $27,500, with a WLTP range of 207 miles (334 km).

By mid-September, reports claimed Volkswagen’s entry-level EV was already essentially sold out across actross all trims, with more than 30,000 orders and a 10-month waitlist.

In a recent development, according to the latest update from German automotive news outlet Edison Media, that number has doubled in about two months, and buyers now face delivery times of up to 21 months for the base ID. Polo Trend. Deliveries for the sporty GTI version are expected to be around seven months.

It has been revealed that “We clearly planned too conservatively,” a VW manager told Edison during an interview. While VW expected about 90 to 95% to choose to lease, the leasing rate is only about 50%.

The larger 52 kWh battery version has also seen higher-than-expected demand, while 90% surprisingly opted to buy the optional €810 ($890) detachable towbar.

As a result, the company is prioritizing higher-margin models, which is likely leading to longer delivery times for the base ID. Polo.

The entry-level variants “just clog up to the line,” Volkswagen’s manager said during the recent interview.

Demand for the ID. Cross, the electric equivalent to Volkswagen’s T-Cross, is also already exceeding expectations.

Cross Life with the 37 kWh battery will go on sale in January 2027, starting at £26,985 ($35,500).

Industry observers note that volkswagen’s newly introduced entry-level electric cars are off to a promising start. The electric urban car family, which includes the ID. Polo, ID. Cross, and the CUPRA Raval and Skoda Epiq, has received nearly 150,000 orders combined since production began in June.

However, the German automaker is still facing an uphill battle. The VW Group posted an operating loss of 5.9 billion euros ($6.5 billion) in the third quarter, its worst quarterly loss since the Dieselgate scandal.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

They may be small, but bear cubs have a pretty steep learning curve. In Alaska, brown bear (Ursus americanus) cubs have a roughly 50 percent survival rate within their first year, while the black bear (Ursus americanus) cub survival rate can range from 51 to 88 percent, depending on where they live. Cubs must learn how to fish, forage, find shelter, and climb trees to escape predators. Fortunately, biology helps out a bit with climbing. Bears have claws that curve and help them go up the tree and then back down safely.

Sources indicate that one baby black bear who spent time at Anan Creek in southeastern Alaska’s Tongass National Forest showed off those climbing chops in style. The park’s rangers have officially awarded this bear with the 2026 Cutest Climber Award.

“This little cub slipped on his way down but caught himself and hustled right after mom,” the rangers write. “An adorable reminder that even when you lose your footing, you can recover and keep going. A tiny, furry lesson in resilience provided by the bears of Anan.”.

Tongass National Forest’s rangers  are at the moment awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

It has been revealed that tongass is the largest national forest in the United States, and covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendanhall Glacier (a popular destination for tourists on Alaskan cruises), numerous hiking trails, eagles soaring above, and plenty of bears on the hunt for food. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska. As such, the creek is a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

In a recent development, according to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears. Similar to  their chunky counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks.

Recent findings suggest that the U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their antics.

The Most Comfortable Sneakers for Women, Tested by a Style Writer

📅 29 Sep 2023 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3119 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in.
  • It has been revealed that at this point, I’m pretty sure I qualify as the woman who lived in her shoes.
  • So, I present to you the pairs of comfortable shoes—think walking shoes and cross-training shoes—that actually keep me feeling comfortable and supported without slacking on cuteness.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

It has been revealed that at this point, I’m pretty sure I qualify as the woman who lived in her shoes. Not in a glamorous Carrie Bradshaw kind of way, but in a professional-sneaker-tester kind of way. I probs have at least 30 pairs crowding my closet and entryways right now, and that’s not even counting the pairs I’ve run into the ground or given away to friends and family (you’re welcome). My top priority is always comfort, and while you might find that a given when it comes to sneakers, I’ve tested my fair share of options that make my feet feel stiff and achy.

So, I present to you the pairs of comfortable shoes—think walking shoes and cross-training shoes—that actually keep me feeling comfortable and supported without slacking on cuteness. From memory foam insoles that mold to your foot's unique shape to running shoes with responsive soles that absorb your stride’s shock, these are the most comfortable sneakers for women, tested by myself and other sneaker enthusiasts at Women’s Health.

The brand ethos of On is to make people feel like they're running on Clouds. It achieves this thanks to its signature Helion Superfoam midsole, which sets itself apart with a construction that blends rigid, stable sections with flexible foam. This combination of materials provides the perfect balance of cushioning and energy return, giving you a bouncy, lightweight feel when your foot hits the pavement. The result is a soft, natural ground feel, rather than an overly bouncy cushioning experience. Fitness contributor Nicolette Accardi notes this tech alone is why this shoe is an absolute workhorse when it comes to running (and running fast!). It’s her all-time favorite race shoe—she even ran a half-marathon in it.

According to Accardi, the shoe feels firm but still has enough flexibility that her running gait isn’t impacted. The toebox has a ton of room for movement, but still holds the foot in place so each step feels responsive and energetic. Even when her legs feel like they’re about to give out, these shoes pick her right back up. On’s innovative speedboard, a flexible plastic plate wedged between the footbed and midsole, snaps back into place for a bouncy effect after your feet hit the ground. This means the shoe requires less energy output with each stride, making running feel easier. Plus, the rebound that comes with the underfoot cushioning gives a spring in your step.

It has been revealed that I might not run marathons like Accardi, but I love to wear this shoe for walking and casual jogs. The CloudTec system, which uses air pockets in the midsole (the layer between the insole and the outsole), to create the shoe’s cushiony feel, propels me forward with every step, kind of like walking on a trampoline. And while it’s great for getting your steps in, this shoe has that chunky look that’s super on trend right now. I love pairing it with tailored pants and a boxy T-shirt on top for that upgraded activewear vibe.

One thing to note, though, is the sole wears down fast, which we found to be disappointing, especially given that price tag. Accardi says the Clifton 10 has a better tread thanks to its thicker outsole designed for high-friction.

Read more: On Cloudmonster 3 Review.

Recent findings suggest that out of all the sneakers I’ve tried, I find myself wearing the Brooks Ghost Max 3—it’s the newest addition to the Ghost Max series—the most when I want to feel comfortable during walks or runs (yep, it can do both!). That’s because the rocker bottom sole, which has a slight curve to it like a rocking chair, helps propel my foot forward with less energy. Wearing it literally feels like walking on pillows.

Sources indicate that with the most cushioning of any shoe on this list (and the most cushioning Brooks offers), it’s perfect for those who need extra support. Fitness contributor Talene Appleton says it has extra plush, foamy cushioning, but even for a max cushioned shoe, it’s incredibly stable thanks to Brooks’ signature Guardrails technology, which is a broad base with two pieces of foam on either side of the heel. It reduces the rolling of the foot both inward and outward, so it cradles your foot in place without messing with your stride. According to Appleton, this combination is great for those with higher arches. After hours of walking, she doesn’t feel an ounce of pain or discomfort. And if you have wide feet or bunions, you’re in luck—this shoe comes in both wide and extra-wide options (huge win!).

Sources indicate that during testing, I did notice that there was some wear and tear on the shoe pretty early on (it had only been a few months of use). The material on the upper of the shoe wore out pretty quickly. While this knocked it down a few points in my book, its supreme comfort still kept this kick at the very top of my list. Plus, I love how many fun colors the shoe comes in—because running and walking should be fun, right?!

Read More: Brooks Ghost Max 3 Review.

Industry observers note that the Hoka Clifton 11 is a standout favorite among WH editors. After testing nearly every Hoka model, I can attest that the Clifton 11 reigns supreme for walking. I was also a fan of the previous Clifton 10, and the newest version feels very similar—just a smidge lighter and more springy. It is by far the most comfortable model in the series to date, and it’s earned a spot in my shoe rotation for its supportive yet flexible cushioning.

Sources indicate that the first major difference I noticed is how light the Clifton 11 feels. Even after wearing it for several hours at a time, it doesn’t feel bulky or clunky. Which makes sense: Hoka did shave nearly half an ounce off the weight compared to the 10. The toe box is slightly narrower, too, but it doesn’t feel tight or uncomfortable. I prefer the more secure fit because it kept my foot from sliding around without feeling cramped. If you like a little more wiggle room for your toes, I would suggest opting for the wide sizing, though.

It has been revealed that despite its lighter weight, it has a generous stack of foam padding throughout the midsole. That weightless yet cushiony feel makes it ideal for my longer walks throughout NYC. The shoe has a mild heel drop (the same as the previous model at 8 mm), which helps distribute pressure evenly across the foot.

I also find that the foam absorbs impact well. My feet—unfortunately plagued by plantar fasciitis—never feel fatigued wearing this shoe. There's technically a rocker shape built into the sole, but it's subtle enough that I barely notice it—instead, my stride feels smooth and natural whether I’m walking or running. I’m also a fan of the durable rubber outsole that gives plenty of traction. I never feel like I’m going to slip while wearing these, even when walking down slippery subway stairs.

So far, the Clifton 11—which was debuted alongside the fresh Clifton Pro— does a great job of keeping my feet comfy and supported. It’s a great shoe for anyone in need of a comfortable, everyday walking sneaker that can also handle the occasional jog (unlike the Clifton Pro, which is geared more toward high-speed running).

Read more: Hoka Clifton 11 and Clifton Pro Review.

Industry observers note that there’s nothing worse than slipping into an uncomfortable shoe after a tough run—that’s where the Alo Recovery Sneaker comes in. Designed to support tired feet, it features a structured sole and high-rebound foam insole that offers arch support and bounces back into place with each step. It makes every step feel stable, cushioned, and balanced. The second I put this pair on after a long run, my feet are instantly relaxed. I can’t say that about most of my other sneakers.

One of the biggest perks of this shoe? The traction is next-level, which is key for a recovery sneaker that’s meant to keep you comfortable and steady all day. Inside, the sock-like lining prevents your foot from sliding around. The thick ankle collar also helps stabilize the foot and provides extra support up the leg, keeping everything locked in place.

It has been revealed that style-wise, this sneaker goes with everything—sweats, shorts, jeans, leggings, you name it. That’s why I crowned it the best overall platform sneaker. After giving it a spin for a few weeks running around Manhattan, walking my dog around Long Island, and wearing it to and from workout classes, it's done the best job at keeping my feet pain-free compared to many other platform sneakers I've worn. The 1.5-inch platform is subtle but adds just the right amount of height to elongate my legs without being so tall that I feel unstable. Oh, and it’s super cute to boot. I’m a massive fan of the Natural White colorway, which looks clean and classic, and pairs effortlessly with everything from sweatpants to denim.

Recent findings suggest that even if you’re not fresh off a run, it works for the office, errands, or a casual lunch. It’s hands down one of the most versatile (and most worn) shoes in my closet. My one con is that it feels a bit heavy and bulky, especially after a long day of wear.

Read more: Alo Recovery Mode Sneaker Review.

Sources indicate that I hadn't tried Asics until this year, and now it's my go-to shoe brand. Not only does its shoe have a streetwear vibe (I'm loving the bright yellow color with sweats and jeans), but they’re also some of the most comfortable shoes I’ve ever worn. In the UB9-S Gel Kayano 20s, the brand uses its signature gel cushioning technology, which features gel units placed in both the heel and forefoot of the shoe to absorb shock and provide a soft landing. This cushioning adapts to your foot’s movement, offering flexibility while reducing impact on your joints. Plus, the form-fitting upper keeps your foot locked in place, making it perfect for long runs, but stylish enough for everyday wear.

I wear this shoe everywhere—on runs, in the gym, and even to the office—and I get compliments virtually every single time I step out in it. The support is unmatched, the traction is solid, and it’s lightweight enough that I never feel weighed down. Plus, it breaks in fast (I wore it right out of the box), so there’s no awkward adjustment period. If you’re looking for a sneaker that can do it all while still looking cool, this is the one for you.

One con to note: It comes in some funky colors, so if you’re not into something bright and fun, I’d recommend looking elsewhere. I also wish it came in a wider version for those with wider feet and bunions.

Read More: Asics Gel-Kayano 20 Review.

We’ve been fans of the Chargefeel line for years, with the previous edition—the Chargefeel 2—winning the best cross-training shoe for our 2025 WH Sneaker Awards. Lululemon has since made a few tweaks that make it even better. “Everyone I know who has worked out in the Chargefeel—myself included—has loved its perfect balance of stability and flexibility,” notes WH executive health and fitness director Jacqueline Andriakos, NASM-CPT.

Recent findings suggest that now with a lighter weight and a lower heel-to-toe drop (6 mm compared to 9.5 mm), the shoe doesn’t weigh me down and puts less stress on the ankles and feet. I’m a significant fan of the wider base for lifting and squatting because it makes my feet feel locked. The forefoot-hugging band on the inside of the shoe and a tough plastic heel counter add extra security, while the springy EVA foam cushioning makes it a workhorse for walking and running.

And post-workout, it’s a great leisure kick for traveling or running errands. I recently wore this sneaker while traveling, and it kept my feet happy power walking through the airport and standing in long security and customs lines. Andriakos agrees, stating, “The stylish silhouette looks good outside the gym.”.

The fit is true to size, and while wide-size options are not available, the toes still have adequate room to spread with each step or lift. However, the wide outsole may feel too bulky during stair climbing or quick, dynamic moves.

Read More: lululemon Chargefeel 3 Review.

In a recent development, let me introduce you to my fresh favorite low-profile, fashion sneaker: the Puma Speedcat. It’s been making waves with style girls, and after testing it out for months, I can see why. This shoe pairs so well with any outfit, with a slim, almost ballet-flat silhouette that doesn’t clash with nicer pieces in my wardrobe. I even see celebs like Em Rata sport the Speedcat all the time, and they always make any streetwear ‘fit look so chic and cool.

According to recent reports, like the Samba, it has a pretty flat sole, but I actually find it more cushioned thanks to its EVA midsole, which has a lightweight, cushioned feel and shock-absorbing properties. This means I can walk around for longer without my feet aching. Plus, after wearing it on wet city streets, I’ve noticed it has better traction, which is a huge win.

The only downside? The fit is a little narrow, especially in the toe area. If you have wider feet, I’d definitely recommend sizing up.

Read More: Puma Speedcat OG Review.

Sources indicate that originally designed for indoor soccer, the Adidas Samba has become a cult-favorite sneaker that’s just as popular on the streets as it is on the field. At first glance, the Samba looks pretty flat, so I wasn’t expecting much in terms of comfort. But after logging hundreds of miles walking around the city, I was surprised by how well it supports my feet. The Samba uses a combination of synthetic leather for the upper and a rubber sole with a cushioned midsole for comfort. The cushioning is more subtle compared to high-performance running shoes, but it still provides a soft, supportive feel. Even without a ton of cushioning, I rarely experience discomfort, which is impressive for a sneaker this sleek. It runs narrow, especially for wide feet, and I recommend going a half size down, as it tends to run big—many with wider feet or bunions agree it’s not the best fit.

It’s a go-to for effortlessly cool outfits—you can wear it with jeans, dresses, slacks, or shorts and always look stylish. I own this shoe in two different colorways (it comes in so many different shades), and after wearing it with practically everything in my closet, I can confidently say it adds a sporty, trendy touch to any outfit.

In a recent development, one of Under Armour’s first-ever shoes, this kick is rooted in sport. But it’s gotten some essential upgrades since its launch, and it’s safe to say I’m hooked. Since 2009, it’s been updated with leather upper overlays to keep the foot supported and soft UA HOVR cushioning, made from soft EVA foam and rubber, which is engineered to store and release energy with each step, providing a bouncy, responsive feel that helps propel you forward. Out of all the shoes I’ve tried, this pair feels the most bouncy, which I know is an absolute essential for the runners and walkers out there that like that super thick underfoot feel. It also has a rocker shape to keep the foot in a forward motion for less energy exertion.

Industry observers note that the UA Apparition also has a mesh upper for supreme breathability—I’ve worn it during HIIT workouts, runs, and walks and never feel like my feet are constricted or sweaty, but I still feel supported and balanced. With a sleek, minimalistic look, the Apparition pairs well with anything from gym gear to casual streetwear. The rubber outsole provides traction and durability, allowing for smooth transitions during both dynamic workouts and everyday use.

My one con? There are some fun colors available, but I wish there were more options to choose from.

Industry observers note that when it comes to comfortable sneakers, cushioning should be your top priority—whether you’re walking, running, hitting the gym, or just running errands. Here are the cushioning levels you can expect to see in the shoes below:.

Recent findings suggest that as Women’s Health editors, we practically live in sneakers, so we know what it takes for a shoe to feel super comfortable. When I originally put together this list of the most comfortable sneakers in 2025, I spent over two years testing more than 50 pairs in every possible scenario—long and short walks, runs, HIIT workouts, full days out in NYC, travel days, and more. For this 2026 enhancement, myself and other WH editors re-tested newer iterations of our favorite pairs to make sure they still meet our standards. I also sought advice from fitness contributors Nicolette Accardi and Talene Appleton, as well as style contributor Lily Wohlner. We looked at everything from cushioning and stability to sizing, traction, and color options. And if a pair left our feet aching or uncomfortable, it didn’t make the cut. So you can trust that every sneaker on this list kept our feet happy all day long—even through our toughest workouts.

#178494. You Know Animal-Print Rugs, But Do You Know Animal Pictorials? (2026)

You Know Animal-Print Rugs, But Do You Know Animal Pictorials? (2026)

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1386 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the oldest known pile rug—pulled from a frozen tomb in Siberia in 1949—features a procession of 24 fallow deer and a parade of men on horseback.
  • Rajaram is describing a literal animal rug, also known as an animal pictorial.
  • “What we’re seeing now is a shift toward rugs where the whole animal is part of the design and has a role in the composition,” indicates Kerri Anne Besse, design director at rug brand Tumble.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the oldest known pile rug—pulled from a frozen tomb in Siberia in 1949—features a procession of 24 fallow deer and a parade of men on horseback. Some 2,500 years after its creation, animal illustrations are making their way back onto the floor. A serpent coils through the Snake and Pomegranate rug by Christopher Farr and Studio Shamshiri in Lucy Hale’s Los Angeles home, and a Tibetan tiger stretches across Demi Lovato’s modern farmhouse and Ethan Cook’s SoHo loft. These aren’t spots or stripes standing in for a neutral—they’re meant to be noticed and discussed. “Animal print is a texture; an animal motif is a story,” notes AD100 designer Pavitra Rajaram, who recently designed Bahaar, an animal-themed rug in her Majnun collection for Jaipur Living. “I think people are tired of decoration that says nothing and are looking for objects that carry meaning.”.

Rajaram is describing a literal animal rug, also known as an animal pictorial. These playful floor coverings often feature a bucolic scene of several animals or a single animal form woven into the textile, and they come in styles ranging from avant-garde and surrealist to Art Deco and folk-inspired.

A master bedroom by Studio Duggan.

“What we’re seeing now is a shift toward rugs where the whole animal is part of the design and has a role in the composition,” indicates Kerri Anne Besse, design director at rug brand Tumble. “The oversized, blown-up animal print feels dated.”.

As for styling, Sophie Salata, head of brand at Vinterior, recommends that designers let the pictorials stand on their own. “I’d be inclined to treat the rug almost as a piece of art, allowing it to become a focal point rather than trying to make everything around it match,” she claims. Pamela Marshall, creative director at artisanal rug brand Patterson Flynn, agrees with this approach: These designs are more than backdrops.

Reformation's nine-piece rug collection with Les Éditions de Tapis includes depictions of cats, swans, and tigers.

It has been revealed that recently, brands have been launching their own interpretations of animal pictorials. Last week, Reformation released its first-ever home collection, a collaboration with Les Éditions de Tapis that features hand-drawn swans and cats. At Milan Design Week this year, Fornasetti launched a surrealist-inspired line of rugs with CC-Tapis depicting slithering serpents from the luxury designer’s archive. A few months earlier, Ruggable released its collaboration with Scalamandré to bring the upscale design house’s iconic zebras to more homes. And in October 2025, Nordic Knots launched its Swedish Grace collection, including the Grace 03 Fauna rug, which shows a wildlife scene. Looking further back, Beni’s serpent rugs have been a designer favorite since 2020.

Industry observers note that one of the earlier examples of literal animal rugs is a collection between longstanding collaborators Patterson Flynn and AD100 designers Charlap Hyman & Herrero. It grew from a one-off rug into a full collection of graphic natural-and-black silhouettes that launched in 2018 and continues to expand. “Areas of inspiration for these come from Calder’s simplified animal forms, the surrealists’ play on scale, and 17th-century cabinets of curiosity, to name a few,” states Marshall, who credits Hyman’s “encyclopedic” design references for the originality. We would be remiss not to mention Diane von Furstenberg’s long-running collaboration with the Rug Firm, which has been producing the iconic Climbing Leopard rug since 2005.

Rugs from Charlap Hyman & Herrero x Patterson Flynn’s collaboration.

The Rug Firm x Diane von Furstenberg Climbing Leopard rug in emerald.

These rugs’ rich history might be part of their renewed appeal. Animals have been a subject for as long as people have made pictures. The oldest known figurative cave painting—found in Indonesia and dated to at least 51,200 years ago—reveals a wild pig with three human figures.

“Animals have shaped our textiles and rugs for longer than we think,” notes Bella Valenzia, founder of Pelican House, pointing out that animal forms have appeared in tapestries and wall coverings, and as functional home objects, such as pelt and hide rugs used for warmth and comfort, since the earliest days of humankind. “We like to think it is part of a wider return to folk-inspired, storytelling textiles, with a sense of nostalgia,” she adds. Pelican House’s rug Frith references the old English countryside, where horses have long been at the heart of rural life.

Various animals, real and mythical, carry their own significance across cultures, and their meaning can deeply influence a home’s design. For example, a pictorial of a lion, which signifies power in certain cultures, adds a very different element to a space than a fish, which can signify good luck, notes Jahanshah “Josh” Nazmiyal of Rug & Kilim. Veronica Renton, senior vintage and antiques specialist at 1stDibs, adds that peacocks often signal nobility and immortality.

According to recent reports, plenty of designers still reach for the originals: While the contemporary versions of these rugs are having a moment, their earlier counterparts remain relevant. “I particularly love antique Tibetan tiger rugs and Persian and Chinese rugs featuring guardian lions, dragons, and all manner of mythical beasts,” says Tiffany Duggan, founder of Studio Duggan.

The Tiger Rug by Studio Ashby in Sophie Ashby’s former home in London.

Where these rugs live in the home is likewise vital. Naturally, the pieces work well in spaces that are meant to be playful, like nurseries and children’s rooms. For example, in this garden apartment designed by Rebecca Benichou and Florence Jallet of Batiik Studio, the Toulemonde Bochart Lion rug brings a spot of levity to a windowless craft room. In the bedroom of Kate Upton and Justin Verlander’s daughter, Genevieve, designed by John Ruggiero, the Doing Goods Blooming Black Bear Rug provides a spot of whimsy. For double the fun, designer Olivia Song put two animal rugs, the Doing Goods Pinky Lion and Pinky Leopard, in her nephew’s room in this Sag Harbor beach home.

That said, these rugs work in more adult spaces, too. “In the [primary] bedroom of one of our London projects, we used the beautiful Snake and Pomegranate rug,” notes Duggan. “I love the way the snake weaves its way around the bed, creating a focal point and bringing a little humor and unexpected character to an otherwise calm space.”.

Designer Rayman Boozer from Apartment 48 has a rug with a large tiger on it from the Rug Company in his own home. “Animal motifs can sometimes feel juvenile, but there’s something refreshing about bringing that sense of playfulness into a sophisticated space,” he notes.

Rayman Boozer’s home, featuring an Apartment 48 tiger rug.

Sources indicate that steven Loloi, co-principal at Loloi, agrees. Speaking of Loloi’s Roam collection that released last month and features cheetahs, zebras, elephants, and giraffes in neutral colors, he highlights the surprising versatility of the pieces, which he says can fit just as nicely in a bedroom or living room as in a lounge or den. “I think we’re seeing people become more confident in their design choices and a little less concerned with playing it safe,” he says. “Why not have a leopard or zebra in your living room?”.

It has been revealed that it’s worth noting that these rugs aren’t for everyone, and some designers avoid any type of animal rug because of the hunting culture they reference. Others, though, embrace them as a way to reimagine humanity’s relationship to animals and commit to living better by them.

Rajaram's Bahaar rug does just that with its contemporary expression of 'shikargahs,' the enclosed forests where kings hunted at leisure, which are celebrated in Iranian and Mughal design. “Instead of being chased, the animals are in harmony with each other, frolicking freely in the forest. It’s a celebration of coexistence rather than conquest,” she says. The Charlap Hyman & Herrero x Patterson Flynn collection had a similar ambition: “Our Tigre and Oso nod to traditional hide floor coverings; they give you the drama of the trophy rug without the trophy,” notes Marshall.

On the surface, the return of these animal-forward rugs might have looked like a change in aesthetics, but it’s really much more anthropological. “We have always gravitated toward pieces with animals, and even in modern production, history is repeating itself,” indicates Nazmiyal. Some 2,500 years after their first spotting, these animal-clad rugs are back home.

It has been revealed that not all commutes are created equal, and tackling a hard commute takes a lot more than a motor and a set of wheels.
